questions.stem: A student measures how the temperature of hydrochloric acid affects the time a strip of magnesium ribbon takes to dissolve. What is the independent variable?
options: The temperature of the acid
The time for the ribbon to dissolve
The concentration of the acid
The mass of the magnesium ribbon
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the experimenter deliberately changes, here the acid's temperature. The dissolving time is the dependent variable, which is measured, and the acid's concentration and the ribbon's mass should be kept constant as controlled variables.

questions.stem: A student investigates how the mass of ethanol burnt affects the temperature rise of 200 g of water. What is the dependent variable?
options: The temperature rise of the water
The mass of ethanol burnt in each trial
The mass of water heated
The type of fuel used
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the one measured in response to the change, here the water's temperature rise. The mass of ethanol is the independent variable, and the mass of water and the type of fuel are kept constant.

questions.stem: In an investigation of how the type of catalyst affects the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, which should be a controlled variable?
options: The volume of oxygen collected in each minute
The time taken to collect 50 mL of oxygen gas
The concentration and volume of the hydrogen peroxide
The type of catalyst that is added to each trial
questions.explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so that only the independent variable, the type of catalyst, can explain differences in rate. The volume of oxygen and the time to collect it are measures of the dependent variable, the rate.

questions.stem: In an investigation of how different catalysts affect the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, why is a trial with no catalyst also run?
options: To keep the temperature the same across all of the trials
To check that each catalyst is not used up by the end of its trial
To find the activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction
To give a baseline showing the effect of adding each catalyst
questions.explanation: The uncatalysed trial is a control: comparing it with the catalysed trials shows how much each catalyst changes the rate. It cannot tell you whether a catalyst is used up, which needs the catalyst's mass to be measured before and after, and it gives no value for the activation energy.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a testable hypothesis?
options: Acids are dangerous chemicals that should always be handled with care
The reaction may or may not speed up at some of the temperatures used
If the acid's temperature is raised, the rate of gas production will increase
Magnesium is a more interesting metal to react with acid than zinc is
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction that links the independent and dependent variables and can be supported or refuted by data. 'More interesting' is an opinion, the safety statement is advice rather than a prediction, and a prediction that allows any outcome cannot be refuted.

questions.stem: In science, accuracy describes:
options: whether a method measures what it is meant to
how close a measurement is to the true value
how close repeated measurements are to each other
the smallest change an instrument can detect
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true or accepted value. Closeness of repeated measurements to each other is precision, the smallest detectable change is resolution, and measuring what is intended is validity.

questions.stem: Four titres of 21.45, 21.50, 21.40 and 21.45 mL are obtained, but the true titre is 23.00 mL. How are these results best described?
options: Neither accurate nor precise
Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
questions.explanation: The titres agree within 0.10 mL of each other, so they are precise, but all are about 1.5 mL below the true value, so they are not accurate. Results like this point to a systematic error.

questions.stem: The resolution of a measuring instrument is:
options: the range of values it is able to measure
how consistent its readings are when repeated
the smallest change in a quantity that it can detect
how close its readings are to the true value of the quantity
questions.explanation: A balance that reads to 0.01 g has a finer resolution than one reading to 0.1 g. How close readings are to the true value is accuracy, and how consistent they are is precision.

questions.stem: A titration result is confirmed by a student at another school using different equipment and a different operator. This shows that the result is:
options: of high resolution
reproducible
repeatable
accurate
questions.explanation: Reproducibility is agreement when the measurement is made under changed conditions, such as a different person, place or equipment. Repeatability is agreement when the same person repeats it with the same method and equipment. Two results agreeing does not show either is close to the true value.

questions.stem: A student compares the energy released by four fuels, each burnt under a can of water. For some fuels the can holds 100 g of water and for others 200 g, and its height above the flame varies. Which statement is correct?
options: The comparison is not valid, as uncontrolled variables could explain the differences
The comparison is valid but not precise, because the masses of water differ
The comparison is valid, provided each fuel is tested at least three times
The comparison is not reproducible, because only one method was used
questions.explanation: A valid comparison changes only the independent variable, the fuel. Changing the mass of water and the distance to the flame changes how much heat is captured, so the differences cannot be attributed to the fuels. Repeating the trials improves precision but cannot fix an invalid design.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a random error?
options: A balance that reads 0.05 g too high for every mass weighed
A pipette that delivers 24.90 mL each time instead of 25.00 mL
Always reading the burette from above the level of the meniscus
Small variations in judging the colour change at the end point
questions.explanation: Random errors vary unpredictably in size and direction from one trial to the next, like small differences in judging an end point. A balance offset, an inaccurate pipette and a consistent parallax error all shift every result in the same direction, so they are systematic errors.

questions.stem: In a calorimetry experiment, a thermometer reads 1.0 °C too high throughout. How does this affect the measured temperature rise, ΔT?
options: ΔT is unaffected, because the offset cancels when the difference is taken
ΔT is 1.0 °C too high, so the calculated energy released is also too high
ΔT is 2.0 °C too high, because both readings are too high
ΔT is 1.0 °C too low, because the starting reading is too high
questions.explanation: Both the initial and final readings are 1.0 °C too high, so subtracting one from the other removes the offset and ΔT is correct. The individual temperatures are inaccurate, but a calculation using only the change is not affected by a constant offset.

questions.stem: How can the effect of random errors on a result be reduced?
options: By using the same instrument for every one of the trials
By rounding the results to fewer significant figures
By repeating the measurements and calculating a mean
By recalibrating the instrument against a standard
questions.explanation: Random errors scatter results both above and below the true value, so averaging many trials tends to cancel them and improves precision. Recalibration targets systematic errors, and rounding only hides the scatter.

questions.stem: How are systematic errors best reduced?
options: By recording results to more decimal places
By calibrating equipment and improving the method
By repeating the whole experiment many more times
By averaging the results from many trials
questions.explanation: A systematic error shifts every result in the same direction, so repeating and averaging leave it in place. It must be found and removed, for example by calibrating the balance or thermometer, or by insulating a calorimeter to reduce heat loss.

questions.stem: While transferring a solution into a volumetric flask, a student spills some of it. How is this best described?
options: A personal error, so that trial should be discarded and repeated
A random error, which averaging with other trials will cancel out
A systematic error, which calibrating the equipment will correct
An uncertainty, which should be included when the mean is found
questions.explanation: A spill is a mistake, or personal error: it is not part of the natural scatter of results and not a fault in the equipment. The affected trial should be recorded in the logbook, excluded and repeated, rather than averaged in.

questions.stem: Titres of 20.10, 20.15, 20.70 and 20.05 mL are recorded. What is the best value for the mean titre?
questions.explanation: 20.70 mL is an outlier, well outside the other three, which agree within 0.10 mL. It is excluded (and noted in the logbook), and the mean of the concordant titres is (20.10 + 20.15 + 20.05) ÷ 3 = 20.10 mL. Including the outlier gives 20.25 mL.

questions.stem: How many significant figures are there in 0.02050?
questions.explanation: Leading zeros only place the decimal point and are not significant, so counting starts at the 2: the digits 2, 0, 5 and the final 0 are significant. The trailing zero after the decimal point shows the measurement was made to that precision.

questions.stem: A student calculates n = cV with c = 0.100 M and V = 0.02316 L. How should the amount be reported?
options: 2 × 10⁻³ mol
questions.explanation: 0.100 × 0.02316 = 0.002316 mol. When multiplying, the answer has as many significant figures as the least precise value, and 0.100 has three, so the answer is 2.32 × 10⁻³ mol. Four figures overstates the precision and two understates it.

questions.stem: The mass of a sample falls from 2.50 g to 2.20 g on heating. What is the percentage change in mass?
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (final − initial) ÷ initial × 100 = (2.20 − 2.50) ÷ 2.50 × 100 = −12.0%. Dividing by the final mass instead of the initial mass gives −13.6%, and 88.0% is the percentage of the mass that remains.

questions.stem: A student's experimental value for the molar heat of combustion of ethanol is 1150 kJ mol⁻¹, and the data book value is 1360 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the percentage difference from the data book value?
questions.explanation: Percentage difference = (1360 − 1150) ÷ 1360 × 100 = 210 ÷ 1360 × 100 = 15.4%, measured against the accepted value. Dividing by the experimental value gives 18.3%, and 84.6% is the experimental value as a percentage of the accepted one.

questions.stem: To find the rate of reaction at a particular time from a graph of volume of gas against time, a student should:
options: divide the volume at that time by the total time since the start
find the area under the curve up to that particular time
join the first and last points and find that line's gradient
draw a tangent to the curve at that time and find its gradient
questions.explanation: The rate at an instant is the gradient of the curve at that point, found from a tangent. Dividing the volume by the time gives the average rate since the start, which is higher than the instantaneous rate on a curve that is levelling off.

questions.stem: Why should the standards for a calibration curve cover the expected concentration of the unknown sample?
options: The gradient of the curve depends on the concentration of the unknown
Reading within the range of standards is more reliable than extrapolating
The curve must pass exactly through the unknown's value to be valid
Standards more concentrated than the unknown always cause systematic error
questions.explanation: Interpolating between known standards relies on the measured relationship, whereas extrapolating assumes it continues unchanged beyond the data, which may not be true. The gradient comes from the standards alone, not from the unknown.

questions.stem: A graph of temperature rise against mass of fuel burnt is a straight line passing through the origin. What does this show?
options: The temperature rise is greatest when the smallest mass of fuel is burnt
The temperature rise is directly proportional to the mass of fuel burnt
The temperature rise is inversely proportional to the mass of fuel burnt
The temperature rise doubles with each additional gram of fuel burnt
questions.explanation: A straight line through the origin means the ratio of temperature rise to mass is constant, so doubling the mass doubles the rise. Inverse proportion would give a curve that falls as the mass increases, and doubling with each extra gram would be an exponential curve.

questions.stem: What information does a safety data sheet (SDS) for a chemical provide?
options: The method for the investigation that is about to be carried out
The results expected when the chemical is used in an experiment
The percentage yield of the chemical in its common reactions
Its hazards, safe handling and storage, first aid and disposal
questions.explanation: An SDS sets out a chemical's hazards and how to handle, store, transport and dispose of it safely, with first aid and spill procedures. Students use it to inform a risk assessment; it does not give the method or results of any particular investigation.

questions.stem: A risk assessment for warming ethanol identifies that it is highly flammable. Which control measure is appropriate?
options: Heat it directly over a Bunsen flame so that it warms quickly
Seal it in a stoppered flask before heating it in a water bath
Wear gloves only, since ethanol vapour does not catch alight
Keep naked flames away and warm it in an electric water bath
questions.explanation: Ethanol vapour ignites easily, so flames must be removed and an electrically heated water bath used. Heating a sealed flask could build up pressure and burst it, and ethanol vapour is flammable, so gloves alone do not control the risk.

questions.stem: How should concentrated sulfuric acid be diluted safely?
options: Mix the acid and water in a sealed bottle
Add the acid slowly to water, stirring
Add water slowly to the acid, stirring
Add the acid quickly to water, stirring
questions.explanation: Dilution releases a lot of heat. Adding acid slowly to a larger volume of water lets the water absorb the heat; adding water to the acid can boil the water locally and spatter concentrated acid. A sealed container could burst.

questions.stem: Which action breaches ethical conduct when reporting an investigation?
options: Acknowledging a classmate who helped to set up the apparatus
Citing a data book as the source of the reference values used
Leaving out results that do not fit the hypothesis without saying so
Recording an outlier in the logbook and explaining why it was excluded
questions.explanation: Silently removing inconvenient data misrepresents the evidence and is dishonest. Excluding an outlier is acceptable when it is recorded and justified, and acknowledging help and citing sources are part of ethical reporting.

questions.stem: Why do VCE Chemistry students keep a logbook during their investigations?
options: It records raw data and method changes as they happen, authenticating the work
It replaces the need to process the data or to draw conclusions from it
It holds only the final processed results that will appear on the poster
It records the teacher's assessment of each of the practical tasks
questions.explanation: The logbook is a dated record of planning, raw data, observations, modifications to the method and preliminary analysis, made as the work is done. This shows the work is the student's own and allows results to be checked.

questions.stem: A student collates published data on the energy densities of different rechargeable batteries to answer a research question. Which investigation methodology is this?
options: Literature review
Fieldwork
Controlled experiment
Product, process or system development
questions.explanation: A literature review collates and analyses secondary data from other people's findings. No primary data is generated, so it is not a controlled experiment or fieldwork, and nothing is being designed or built.

questions.stem: A student measures nitrate concentrations at several sites along a local creek. Which investigation methodology is this?
options: Simulation
Classification and identification
Fieldwork
Literature review
questions.explanation: Fieldwork involves generating site-specific primary data at a particular location, with the site's context recorded in the logbook. A literature review uses only secondary data, and a simulation studies a system through a model rather than at the real site.

questions.stem: Which statement is evidence rather than opinion?
options: A website states that catalysts are always worth paying the extra cost for
Over five trials, the catalysed reaction gave 50 mL of oxygen in a mean of 32 s
Manganese dioxide is clearly the best catalyst that anyone could choose to use
Most of the students in the class think that enzymes work better than metal oxides
questions.explanation: Evidence is data gathered systematically that others could check or repeat. A personal judgement, a show of hands and an unsupported claim on a website are opinions or anecdote, however confidently they are stated.

questions.stem: A student measures a reaction's rate at 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C, with one trial at each, and the rate rises each time. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hypothesis is proven true, so no further trials are needed to support it
Rate rose with temperature from 20 to 50 °C, but repeats are needed to judge precision
Rate rises with temperature at every temperature, so heating it always helps
Temperature is the only factor that affects the rate of this particular reaction
questions.explanation: A conclusion should stay within the range tested and acknowledge limitations, here the single trial at each temperature. The data say nothing about temperatures outside 20–50 °C or about other factors, and evidence can support a hypothesis but never prove it.

questions.stem: A student's results contradict the hypothesis. What should the student do?
options: Discard the results, because a carefully reasoned hypothesis cannot be wrong
Report that the evidence does not support the hypothesis and suggest why
Rewrite the hypothesis to match the results, without mentioning the change
Repeat the experiment until the results come out supporting the hypothesis
questions.explanation: A refuted hypothesis is a valid scientific outcome. The student should report it honestly, discuss possible reasons such as errors or flawed assumptions, and suggest further investigation. Repeating until the 'right' answer appears is biased selection of data.

questions.stem: What is a limitation of the lock-and-key model of enzyme action?
options: It shows the active site as rigid, but it changes shape slightly on binding
It cannot explain why an enzyme is specific to one particular substrate
It treats enzymes as carbohydrates when they are in fact proteins
It shows the substrate binding at a site away from the active site
questions.explanation: Real active sites are flexible and adjust a little as the substrate binds, which the rigid lock-and-key picture does not show. The model's strength is that it does explain specificity, since only a matching shape fits the active site.

questions.stem: A calibration equation, peak area = 7.5 × concentration, is used to predict the concentration of caffeine in a drink. What kind of model is this?
options: A case study
A mathematical model
A physical scale model
A conceptual model
questions.explanation: A mathematical model describes a relationship between variables with an equation that can be used to make predictions. A physical model is a scaled representation of an object, such as a molecular model kit, and a conceptual model represents a system through ideas and diagrams.

questions.stem: How does a linear economy differ from a circular economy? A linear economy:
options: makes, uses and then disposes of products as waste
keeps materials in use by reusing and recycling them
makes all its products from renewable feedstocks
designs its products to be repaired, not replaced
questions.explanation: A linear economy follows a take–make–dispose path, so materials end as waste. A circular economy keeps materials in use for as long as possible through reuse, repair and recycling, which reduces waste and the demand for new raw materials.

questions.stem: A government declines to fund a green hydrogen plant despite strong evidence of its environmental benefits, citing its cost to taxpayers. This decision is based mainly on:
options: economic factors, not solely on scientific evidence
ethical factors about the use of human research subjects
legal factors that follow from the laws of thermodynamics
scientific evidence that the plant could never work
questions.explanation: The scientific evidence favoured the plant, but the decision turned on cost, which is an economic factor. Decisions about chemistry-related issues often weigh sociocultural, economic, political, legal and ethical factors alongside the science.

questions.stem: A student's titres vary by up to 0.6 mL. Which change is most likely to improve their precision?
options: Adding titrant dropwise near the end point and reading the burette at eye level
Filling the burette with a larger volume of the standard solution each time
Measuring the aliquot with a beaker rather than with a calibrated pipette
Calculating the mean titre to two more decimal places than before
questions.explanation: Overshooting the end point and inconsistent reading of the meniscus cause scatter, so adding titrant slowly near the end point and reading at eye level makes titres agree more closely. A beaker measures volume far less precisely than a pipette, and extra decimal places do not reduce scatter.

questions.stem: A burette reading has an uncertainty of ±0.05 mL. Which change reduces the percentage uncertainty in the titre?
options: Using a measuring cylinder instead of the burette
Using a more dilute titrant, so that a larger titre is needed
Using a smaller aliquot, so that a smaller titre is needed
Reading the burette to one fewer decimal place each time
questions.explanation: The absolute uncertainty stays at about ±0.05 mL whatever the titre, so a larger titre makes it a smaller percentage: ±0.05 mL is 0.5% of 10 mL but 0.2% of 25 mL. A smaller titre raises the percentage uncertainty, and a measuring cylinder is far less precise.

questions.stem: Five trials of a spirit-burner experiment give heats of combustion that agree closely with each other but are all about 30% below the data book value. What is the best explanation?
options: Poor resolution of the balance, as all five of the trials agree with each other
A systematic error such as heat loss, as the results are precise but inaccurate
Random error, as the five results are precise and consistent with each other
A mistake in one trial, as a single outlier has pulled the mean value down
questions.explanation: Results that agree with each other but are all shifted in one direction indicate a systematic error; in an open calorimeter, heat lost to the surroundings is the usual cause. Random error produces scatter, and a single outlier could not make all five results low.
